1:
What was in the vial divides them, and both sides think it obvious. Henry says it was common oil, no doubt, and that we read of no blessing or prayer over it; Gill reports the Jewish view that the tabernacle's anointing oil was at a distant place and reserved for the kings of David's house, so this was common oil, or oil of balsam. Ellicott says the opposite with equal confidence: it was of course no common oil on so momentous an occasion, but the sacred anointing oil used at the consecration of the priests and of the tabernacle. Both take the vessel for a portent, observing that Saul and Jehu were anointed from a vial and reigned briefly while David and Solomon were anointed from a horn and reigned long. Henry presses it: the vessel brittle because the kingdom would soon be cracked and broken, the quantity small because Saul had little of the Spirit compared with David.

The kiss divides them as sharply. Wesley takes it as a testimony of Samuel's sincere friendship and affection. Ellicott denies it flatly: it is rather a customary sign of reverential homage, since at that early date of their acquaintance it was hardly possible to suppose the old man felt affection for the younger. Henry takes it both ways, as approbation and as homage, and sharpens the concession by noting that Samuel was satisfied in a choice which abridged his own power and eclipsed his family's glory.

Clarke keeps his eye on the title. Even here Saul is not acknowledged as king but simply as a captain, one who goes before and leads the people, and Clarke marvels at how simple the ancient ceremony was: oil poured, a kiss, and a sentence. Henry hears the same word as a warning, that a commander bespeaks honour and power but a commander in war bespeaks care and toil and danger, and Wesley draws from "his inheritance" that the people were not so much Saul's as God's, so he was to rule not by his own will but by God's. Ellicott adds a structural observation: anointing is recorded only of David, Absalom, Solomon, Joash, Jehoahaz and Jehu, all founders of dynasties or irregularly advanced, because in a regular succession the original anointing was held to continue its effect and no new one was needed.

The signs bring the commentators onto textual ground. Nobody can identify Zelzah; Clarke and Ellicott both notice that the Greek took the word for a verb and rendered it dancing or springing vehemently, Clarke wondering whether that refers to the joy of finding the asses or to the religious exultation of the following verses, Ellicott reporting the alternative that it means in great haste. Ellicott adds that some have supposed the place to be Zela in Benjamin, where the bodies of Saul and Jonathan were eventually buried. On the terebinth of Tabor Ellicott passes on the conjecture that Tabor is a variant of Deborah and the tree the one under which Rachel's nurse was buried; Delitzsch rejects it outright as having no foundation to rest upon.

Clarke explains the salutation from Eastern custom: the greeting is answered by its mirror, and to give the one and not receive the other is to expect hostility, so the three men are friends. Henry finds two morals in the loaves: they look now like the relieving of a beggar, so Saul must remember he once received alms and be charitable to the poor, but as the first tribute paid to a newly anointed king they might also admonish him not to spend the wealth of his crown in luxury. On the first sign Henry is grimmer: the first place Samuel sent him to was a sepulchre, where a man with a crown in his eye must think of the grave in which all his honour would be laid in the dust.
5:
Four places are proposed for the hill of God. Gill reports the Targum's identification with the hill where the ark stood, which the Jewish commentators generally follow, but argues for Geba, since Saul must by now have passed out of Judah into Benjamin, was near the end of his journey and among his relations, and since a Philistine garrison stood at Geba. Clarke repeats the Targum and adds a height near Gibeah on Calmet's authority. Ellicott and Delitzsch agree on a simpler answer: the phrase should be rendered the Gibeah of God, a proper name for Saul's own town, later called Gibeah of Saul, which took the name from a well-known high place beside it.

What the company of prophets was is the largest question here, and Clarke and Ellicott converge from different directions: both deny these men were prophets in the received sense. Clarke reports the Targum's "company of scribes" and supposes them scholars of the prophets under a teacher probably not himself inspired; Ellicott calls it a grave mistake to conclude that all or even most of the young men trained in these schools were inspired at all, since true prophets were very rare, one or two in a generation, and the schools were founded to foster what we should call the higher education in Israel rather than to produce seers. Clarke then redefines the word itself. Abraham is called a prophet at Genesis 20:7 in a sentence glossing it as praying for another, so the word means a man well acquainted with God, able to teach others, and above all a man of prayer; and it is through inattention to this sense, Clarke says, that every commentator he has met has been sadly puzzled by Saul's prophesying. On his reading it can mean no more than prayer and supplication with hymns of praise, clinched by the observation that not one syllable of any prediction by Saul is preserved.

The ecstasy is approached from opposite sides and neither closes with it. Ellicott insists it would be a mistake to attribute that condition to the schools' carefully cultivated music, and admits we know very little of the state or what produced it. Delitzsch raises the natural explanation only to reject it, quoting the observation that ecstatic states are infectious and spread involuntarily, as in the American revivals and the preaching mania in Sweden, even to those with no affinity for them, then insisting that here there was something more than psychical infection.

"Turned into another man" is graded four ways. Wesley makes it natural endowment, a sudden gift of skill in divine things with courage, wisdom and magnanimity befitting the dignity. Delitzsch is careful: not regeneration in the Christian sense, but a change resembling regeneration which affected the entire disposition of mind. Ellicott is warmest, holding that God changed the heart and finding the proof in Saul's silence afterwards, no exultation and no impatience, his lips sealed even through the drawing of the lots. Henry is coolest: Saul became another man, but whether a new man may be questioned.

The seven days at Gilgal divide them entirely. Clarke refers the command to the sacrifice after the defeat of the Ammonites. Ellicott concedes the chronological difficulties, that two years or more elapsed and this was not the first meeting there, but still refers the warning forward to the later trial, supposing it was repeated in fuller form nearer the time. Gill and Wesley take it for neither occasion but a standing rule, that whenever a great difficulty arose Saul should resort to Gilgal and wait seven days, Wesley adding that the place was chosen for its associations with the covenant and its convenience to the tribes on both sides of Jordan. Delitzsch leaves it grammatically open, since the verb may continue the imperative before it or stand independently as a condition.
9:
Henry fills out what the new heart amounted to. Seeking the asses is quite out of Saul's mind; he thinks now of fighting the Philistines, redressing the grievances of Israel and making laws. He has no longer the heart of a husbandman, low and narrow and concerned only about his corn and cattle, but the heart of a statesman, a general, a prince. Delitzsch notes only that the Hebrew is a pregnant expression, God changed him and gave him another heart, and that Saul could reach Gibeah in a day, Rachel's tomb being four hours off. Ellicott times the two gifts against each other: the new heart was given in the early morning as Saul left Ramah, and that changed heart was a fit home for the Spirit that came on him in the eventide as he drew near his own city.

Why only the third sign is narrated is answered twice: Delitzsch because it caused a great sensation at Gibeah, Wesley because the first two were transient acts passing in private between two or three people while this was permanent and notorious, done before many witnesses. Gill and Henry agree that the gift did not last. Gill cites Procopius Gazaeus that Saul had not the gift always, and that like the prophesying of the seventy elders it was meant to make him respectable so the people would the more readily receive him as king; Henry says the Spirit came strongly and suddenly, as the word signifies, but not so as to rest and abide upon him.

"But who is their father?" is the chapter's most disputed clause, and they split on both its sense and its text. Delitzsch rules out the rendering "who is their instructor" as a gratuitous question and takes it to mean "is their father a prophet, then?" - have they the prophetic spirit by right of birth? If they received it as a free gift, the Lord could give it to Saul as freely. Ellicott reaches the same sense by a small drama: the first citizen is surprised that so undistinguished a man as Kish should have a son among the prophets, and the second points at the singers on the hillside to say they owe their gift to no accident of birth either. Henry offers precisely the reading Delitzsch dismisses, asking whether the father meant is God, or Samuel, under whose roof Saul had lain the night before. The text divides them too: Delitzsch rejects the alteration of "their father" to "his father" which the Greek, Latin and Syriac support, while Clarke reports the same Greek addition, naming Kish, and judges that it makes the sense more complete.

On the proverb Henry and Ellicott arrive independently at the same New Testament parallel, both hearing behind "Is Saul also among the prophets?" the astonishment of those who found the later Saul preaching the gospel he had persecuted. They differ on its origin: Henry takes it from this occasion, Ellicott from the recurrence of the scene later in the book. Henry draws the double moral: the worst are not to be despaired of, yet an external show of devotion and a sudden change for the present are not to be relied on, since Saul among the prophets was Saul still.

Saul's silence afterwards is read variously. Delitzsch attributes it to unambitious humility and denies it was fear of unbelief and envy; Henry finds in it humility, prudence, since a man who proclaimed such news would be envied, and dependence on God, since Saul leaves it to Samuel to carry the work forward and sits still to see how the matter will fall. On the visit to the high place Ellicott has him alone, conscious of the change and desiring solitary communing in a quiet sanctuary; Wesley has him returning there with the prophets to praise God and beg counsel for the business before him.
17:
Why Mizpeh, and in what sense the people gathered "unto the Lord", are answered together. Delitzsch and Ellicott both say Samuel chose it for the memory of the victory he had won there by prayer. On the phrase itself Gill reports that the priest may have been present with the Urim and Thummim and the ark brought up, Ellicott takes the Urim to be meant, and Delitzsch points to the altar that stood at Mizpeh. Gill then deflates the question: wherever the people of God are solemnly gathered in his name, there the Lord is.

Ellicott's handling of the rebuke concedes half the case against himself. It was perfectly true, he says, that in Israel's circumstances a mortal king was needful for the development of the nation's power; but no such change would ever have been necessary had the nation not forsaken its Eternal Sovereign, and it would cost for ever a higher blessedness. Henry has no such balance: those who live better by sense than by faith and lean on an arm of flesh forsake a fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. Delitzsch quotes the judgment that Samuel charged them again to show how dangerous the way was and how bitterly they might yet repent of it.

Why cast lots when Samuel had already anointed the man is answered three ways that amount to one. Henry says Samuel knew the peevishness of the people and that some would not acquiesce in his single testimony, so every tribe should have its chance and the lot would cause contentions to cease. Wesley says it more briefly, that all might know God had chosen Saul. Ellicott puts it higher: the private interview with the seer did not suffice, and the Spirit must choose Saul out publicly, in solemn national assembly. Clarke sets out the machinery in four stages, tribe, thousand, family and man; Ellicott observes that the method is not stated, and that though lots were usually cast by throwing tablets, the Hebrew word here suggests drawing from an urn.

That the lot fell on Benjamin strikes both Henry and Wesley as ominous. Henry notes that anyone who knew the scriptures could foresee a family soon to be put down, since dying Jacob had entailed the dominion on Judah, which must rule as a lion while Benjamin should only ravin as a wolf. Wesley makes the reasoning explicit: the kingdom was freely promised to Judah and to be given him in love, but this one was in a manner forced from God and given in anger, and so conferred on an obscure tribe.

Why Saul hid is answered four ways. Clarke says modesty or fear, Wesley a sense of his own unworthiness, Ellicott a certainty so complete after the signs that he shrank from hearing the lot read out. Henry alone treats it as a reasoned refusal and gives four grounds: Saul knew himself unfit, bred to neither books nor arms nor courts; he foresaw the envy of neighbours already ill-affected to him; he had learned from Samuel that the people sinned in asking a king and that it was granted in anger; and the Philistines were strong and the Ammonites threatening, so he must be bold indeed who would set sail in a storm.

On the stature they agree but differ in manner. Henry has Saul standing in the crowd like a cedar among shrubs, Samuel inviting the people to judge with their own eyes. Ellicott reaches for comparison, noting that Agamemnon too stood head and shoulders above his people, that in one later tradition his name is almost lost and he is known only as the tall one, and that Hebrew song called him the gazelle, the glory of Israel. Against giant Philistines, he concludes, a giant king was needed; the time of the stripling from the house of Jesse was near but not yet come.
25:
What Samuel wrote in the book divides them sharply: did the document threaten the people with despotism or protect them from it? Gill reports two readings: one making it the power a king had over his people and the punishment he might inflict if they rebelled, the other taking it for the arbitrary-power speech of the earlier chapter, written down as a testimony against them, as Josephus also says. Ellicott takes it the other way entirely: the roll set out the right and duties of the God-appointed king and clearly marked the limits of his power, since the vice-gerent of the invisible King could be no arbitrary despot. Wesley agrees, making it the laws and rules by which the kingly government was to be managed. Henry holds both at once. His own reading is constitutional: Samuel had already told them the manner of the king, how he would abuse his power, and now tells them the manner of the kingdom, what power the prince might challenge and the utmost the subject might claim, fixing the land-marks between them. But he then reports the contrary opinion, that Samuel registered the warning so it might hereafter witness that they had drawn the calamity on themselves. Clarke splits the difference by supposing a compact or covenant between the people and Saul.

Ellicott builds a great deal on the same roll. He supposes it also held the details of how the seer came to anoint the Benjamite, and concludes that the compiler of this book drew his knowledge of the choice of Saul from that archive. He goes further still and calls the writing the first trace of literary composition among the Israelites since the days of Moses, crediting the revival of letters that began soon after Saul to Samuel and the schools he founded.

The band that went with Saul is read four ways. Clarke denies it was a military body and takes them for secret friends personally attached to him, rejecting the view that all the men fit to bear arms are meant as inconsistent with Saul's return to his farm. Ellicott makes them fellow citizens proud of the honour done one of their own, guessing that the distinguished men later found about Saul were among them. Wesley reduces them to an escort who gave him safe and honourable conduct home but did not stay. Henry makes them a remnant whose hearts God had touched: if the heart bends the right way at any time it is because he has touched it, and one touch is enough when it is divine.

On the withheld presents Delitzsch and Ellicott agree these were the customary gift on entering a king's presence, so refusing them came near to rebellion. Clarke reads them as tribute, comparing the Arab chiefs still supplied by the free-will offerings of the villages where they encamp, and supposing most people assumed a king meant taxes while these men refused to pay. Gill and Ellicott agree who they were, men of larger tribes and better families who envied an upstart, Ellicott adding that Benjamin had been almost destroyed in the civil war closing Judges. Henry finds the motive elsewhere: these were probably the people most earnest for a king in the first place, who quarrelled with the one they got because he was not such a one as themselves, and disliked him because others did not.

Saul's silence is admired by all, but Henry alone turns it into an argument. Delitzsch renders the phrase "as being deaf", Clarke calls it prudence in not assuming at once all the consequence his office allowed, Ellicott sees great self-control in the new king and his counsellors; Henry reads it as evidence of title, since those are commonly most jealous of their honour and most revengeful of affronts who gain their power by improper means.
